title: Luke
subtitle: An orderly account, so that you may know how firm it is
lead: Luke is the longest of the four Gospels and the first half of a two-volume work whose second half is Acts. It tells the story of Jesus from the announcement of John the Baptist's birth in the temple to Jesus' ascension near Bethany, written for a man named Theophilus so that he could know how sure and firm the teaching he had received really was (1:1–4).

Luke writes as a historian in the Greek manner, with a polished preface, dates tied to emperors and governors, and a careful order. But his story is told in the language of Israel's Scriptures, and it begins and ends in the temple. It gives us much that no other Gospel has: the births of John and Jesus, the Magnificat and the other songs, the shepherds, Jesus at twelve, the good Samaritan, the lost son, the rich man and Lazarus, Zacchaeus, the criminal on the cross, and the road to Emmaus.

Its great themes are God's faithfulness to Israel and his salvation for the nations, good news for the poor and a warning to the rich, the Holy Spirit, prayer, joy, meals, women who follow Jesus, and "today": the moment when God's promises arrive.
facts: Anonymous in the text. From the late 100s the church named Luke, the doctor and traveling companion of Paul (Colossians 4:14). Many critical scholars think of an unknown Gentile Christian of the next generation.
Uncertain. Most scholars: about AD 80–90, after Mark and after the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. Some: the early 60s, before Paul's death. A few: the early 100s.
Unknown. An early prologue says Achaia (Greece); Antioch, Rome and Asia Minor are also proposed.
A Gospel written in the manner of Greek history and biography, the first of two volumes (Luke-Acts).
Greek, the most literary of the Gospels: a classical preface (1:1–4), Bible-style Greek modeled on the Septuagint in chapters 1–2, and polished Greek throughout.
authorship: The Gospel names no author, but the tradition is early and unanimous. Irenaeus (about AD 180) says that Luke, the companion of Paul, set down in a book the gospel Paul preached (Against Heresies 3.1.1). The Muratorian Fragment (probably late 100s) names Luke the physician, who had not seen the Lord in the flesh, and the so-called Anti-Marcionite Prologue adds that he was a Syrian of Antioch, unmarried, who died at eighty-four in Boeotia. The New Testament names a Luke as "the dear doctor" and Paul's fellow worker (Colossians 4:14; Philemon 24; 2 Timothy 4:11), and the "we" passages of Acts (Acts 16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16) seem to place the author at Paul's side.

Many scholars think the author was an unknown Christian writing a generation after Paul. They point to differences between Acts' picture of Paul and Paul's letters (for example on the Jerusalem meeting, Galatians 2 and Acts 15), and to the possibility that the "we" passages come from a source or are a literary convention. Others, including Joseph Fitzmyer and many conservative scholars, accept that a companion of Paul named Luke wrote both books; the tradition attached the work to a minor figure, which is hard to explain unless it was true. The argument that Luke's vocabulary is especially medical (W. K. Hobart, 1882) was answered by Henry Cadbury, who showed that other educated writers used the same words.

About AD 140 Marcion used a shorter Gospel close to Luke, without chapters 1–2 and other passages, which Irenaeus and Tertullian (Against Marcion 4) said he had cut down from Luke. A minority of recent scholars (Matthias Klinghardt, Jason BeDuhn) argue that Marcion's Gospel came first and that our Luke expanded it; most specialists, including Dieter Roth, who reconstructed Marcion's text, still hold that Marcion edited Luke. This is labeled here as a minority view.

Most scholars date Luke about AD 80–90: it uses Mark (usually dated near AD 70), and its sayings about Jerusalem surrounded by armies (21:20) and its enemies building a siege wall (19:43) seem to look back on AD 70. Some (Adolf von Harnack in his later work, and many conservative scholars) date it in the early 60s, because Acts ends with Paul alive in Rome about AD 62 and does not mention his death or the temple's destruction. A few (Richard Pervo, Joseph Tyson) place Luke-Acts in the early 100s.

audience.to: Theophilus, a man of rank addressed as "most excellent" (1:3), and through him Christians in the cities of the Roman Empire a generation or two after Jesus, most of them probably Gentiles, some of them "those who fear God" who had been drawn to the synagogue before believing in Jesus. They spoke Greek, needed Palestinian places and customs explained, knew the Scriptures in the Greek Old Testament, and included rich and poor, men and women.
audience.why: So that Theophilus would know how sure and firm the teaching he had received really was (1:4). Luke answers questions such a church faced: Is this new movement truly the fulfillment of Israel's Scriptures, though most of Israel did not accept it? Why are Gentiles included? Is the movement dangerous to Rome? What do wealth and poverty mean for disciples? Knowing the audience explains Luke's care to tie Jesus to world history (2:1; 3:1), his portrait of faithful Jews welcoming Jesus (1–2; 24:53), his repeated notes that Roman officials found Jesus and Paul innocent (23:4, 14, 22; Acts 26:31–32), and his sharp words to the rich.
views: Most scholars: a Christian, perhaps the patron who paid for the book's copying, who had been "instructed" in the faith (1:4) and needed assurance.

Some: the verb in 1:4 can mean "informed"; Theophilus may have been an interested outsider or a Roman official who had heard reports about the Christians. "Most excellent" is Luke's title for Roman governors (Acts 23:26; 24:3; 26:25).

Many scholars think Luke wrote for Christians generally, not for one community, with Theophilus as dedicatee in the custom of the time (compare Richard Bauckham's argument that the Gospels were written for all Christians).
Most see a mainly Gentile readership. Others (Jacob Jervell) argue that Luke-Acts addresses Jewish Christians and God-fearers concerned with Israel's place in God's plan.

outline: The births and childhoods of John and Jesus
John's preaching, Jesus' baptism, genealogy and testing
Jesus in Galilee: the Nazareth sermon, healings, the Twelve, the Sermon on the Plain English Translation, Peter's confession, the transfiguration
The journey to Jerusalem: teaching, parables, controversy
The supper, arrest, trials and crucifixion
The empty tomb, Emmaus, the appearances and the ascension

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads Luke against the Roman world it names: Augustus' census and Quirinius, Herod the Great and his sons, Tiberius' fifteenth year, Pilate, Galilee and Judea, Samaritans, the temple and its courts, and Roman law in the trials.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the Gospel was made: Luke's use of Mark, the material he shares with Matthew (Q, or Luke's use of Matthew), his own special material ("L"), the claim of the prologue (1:1–4), the date, the unity of Luke and Acts, and the history of the birth stories.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads Luke as a crafted story: a classical prologue, then Bible-style Greek in chapters 1–2, the long journey to Jerusalem (9:51–19:44), reversals of rich and poor, meals, prayer, the Holy Spirit, joy, "today," and the parallels Luke draws with Acts.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads Luke inside Second Temple Judaism: a Gospel that begins and ends in the temple (1:9; 24:53), with Torah-keeping families and Pharisees who invite Jesus to dinner, using Jewish scholars on Luke (Amy-Jill Levine and others), and notes honestly how passages were later read against Jews.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: How the church fathers, the liturgy and the churches have read the passage: the Hail Mary and the daily canticles (Magnificat, Benedictus, Nunc Dimittis), Luke as the evangelist of the poor and of mercy, the parables in preaching, the ox among the four living creatures, and the legend of Luke as painter of Mary.

sections.b: Luke is a story with a plan. It moves from the temple (1:5–23) through Galilee to Jerusalem and back to the temple (24:53), and its middle third is a long journey to Jerusalem that begins when Jesus "fixed his face firmly" on going there (9:51). Read it with Acts: the Gospel ends with the promise of "power from on high" (24:49), and Acts begins with the same scene and carries the message "as far as the farthest end of the earth" (Acts 1:8). Watch for Luke's pairs (a man and a woman: Zechariah and Mary, Simeon and Anna, the lost sheep and the lost coin), his reversals (the lowly raised, the mighty brought down), his meals, and his "today."

Luke says he is not the first to write (1:1). On the majority view he used Mark, following its order for much of 3:1–24:12 and often polishing its Greek, and a collection of sayings he shares with Matthew (called Q); on the Farrer view he used Matthew directly. About a third of the Gospel, including many of the best-loved parables, is found only in Luke (scholars call it "L"). Some think Luke first wrote a draft from Q and L ("Proto-Luke") and added Mark later. See the topic The Synoptic Problem; this page does not repeat it.

Most scholars, following Henry Cadbury, read Luke and Acts as one work in two volumes, written by one author for Theophilus (Luke 1:1–4; Acts 1:1). The two are built in parallel: Jesus and his followers are anointed by the Spirit, preach, heal, are opposed, go to Jerusalem and stand trial; Jesus' and Stephen's dying prayers match (Luke 23:34, 46; Acts 7:59–60). Simeon's song of light for the nations (Luke 2:32) and Paul's last words (Acts 28:28) frame the whole.

Luke 1–2 is written in a different style from the rest of the Gospel, and many think it was composed or added separately. Its historical value is debated. Defenders point to its Jewish detail and to its agreement with Matthew on the main facts. Critics point to its Old Testament patterns and to the census under Quirinius (2:1–2), which Josephus dates to AD 6, ten years after Herod's death. The chapter pages give the views fairly.

Luke is often called the Gospel of the poor. Mary sings that God fills the hungry and sends the rich away empty (1:53); Jesus reads that he has come "to bring good news to the poor" (4:18); his blessings are for the poor and his woes for the rich (6:20–26); and parables found only in Luke warn against wealth (12:13–21; 16:19–31). Zacchaeus shows a rich man's repentance (19:1–10). Readers differ on whether Luke's poor are mainly the materially poor (liberation theology's "preferential option for the poor") or the humble who depend on God; most agree Luke means both and that his warnings to the rich are not merely spiritual.

Luke names more women than any other Gospel: Elizabeth, Mary and Anna (1–2), the widow of Nain (7:11–17), the woman who anointed Jesus' feet (7:36–50), Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna and others who supported Jesus from their own means (8:1–3), Martha and Mary (10:38–42), the bent woman (13:10–17) and the women at the cross and tomb (23:49, 55–24:11). He often pairs a story about a man with one about a woman. Some scholars see Luke as unusually favorable to women; others note that his women mostly serve, listen and support rather than preach, and debate whether Luke widens or limits their roles.

Luke's opening chapters gave the church the Hail Mary, the Magnificat, Benedictus and Nunc Dimittis, the Gloria, Christmas and the Presentation, and the image of Mary pondering. Its parables shaped preaching on mercy and repentance. Among the four living creatures Luke is pictured as the ox. A tradition first reported in the 500s made Luke a painter of icons of Mary, which made him the patron of painters; historians treat this as legend. His feast is October 18.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a Gospel that teaches its reader to wait
spec.body:
Luke's first two chapters are full of people waiting: the people praying outside the sanctuary (1:10, 21), Elizabeth hidden for five months (1:24), Simeon waiting for Israel's comfort (2:25), Anna praying night and day (2:37), and those looking for Jerusalem's redemption (2:38). The Gospel ends with the disciples told to "remain in the city" until they are dressed in power (24:49), and Acts opens with them waiting and praying (Acts 1:4, 14).

My suggestion is that Luke deliberately trains Theophilus to read his own time as a time of faithful waiting: the promises have been kept in Jesus, yet their full outworking (Israel's redemption, the kingdom) is still awaited (Acts 1:6–7). The "certainty" of 1:4 would then be the security of people who have seen enough of God's faithfulness to keep waiting. Hans Conzelmann famously argued that Luke adjusted Christian hope to a delayed end; my reading overlaps with his in seeing waiting as central but differs in finding its pattern already in Israel's faithful remnant in chapters 1–2, not as a later correction.

prompts: A hand-drawn scene sketched onto an old parchment scroll in ink and earth tones: an elderly Jewish priest in white linen stands beside a small golden altar with smoke of incense rising, startled as a tall angel of light appears to the right of the altar; through an opening, a crowd prays in a courtyard. Mix of ancient manuscript illumination, cave-drawing simplicity and modern line art; soft torn edges, no hard rectangle, warm candlelight tones.

A sketch on a weathered scroll: in the hill country of Judea, an older pregnant woman embraces a young pregnant girl at the doorway of a stone house; olive trees and terraced hills behind; the older woman's hand on her own belly as if feeling a leap. Ink lines and washed color, manuscript and modern art mixed, soft vignette edges, no frame.

Night sky on an old scroll: shepherds with a small flock on a rocky hillside near a village of flat-roofed houses, looking up at a blaze of light and a crowd of angel figures drawn like cave-art outlines in gold; below, in the village, a faint glow from a house where animals are kept at one end. Rough charcoal and gold leaf, ancient and modern styles combined, soft irregular edges.

A temple court sketched on parchment: an old man lifts a swaddled baby in his arms, his hands covered with his cloak, while a young mother and a carpenter with two small doves in a cage look on, and an aged woman in a widow's shawl raises her hands in thanks. Iconic simplicity mixed with modern line drawing; muted ochres and blues; edges fading into the scroll.
reading: Joseph A. Fitzmyer, The Gospel According to Luke (Anchor Bible, 2 vols.)
A detailed critical commentary with a long introduction; Catholic, widely respected.
Raymond E. Brown, The Birth of the Messiah
The standard study of Matthew 1–2 and Luke 1–2, fair to every view.
Joel B. Green, The Gospel of Luke (NICNT)
A literary and theological reading of Luke as a whole story.
Luke Timothy Johnson, The Gospel of Luke (Sacra Pagina)
A readable commentary attentive to Luke's literary art and to Acts.
Amy-Jill Levine and Ben Witherington III, The Gospel of Luke
A Jewish and a Christian scholar read Luke together, often disagreeing in the open.
Kenneth E. Bailey, Jesus through Middle Eastern Eyes
Village culture and the parables of Luke, by a scholar who lived in the Middle East for decades.
